title: Ignition is a runaway: heat released grows faster than heat lost, and the figure shows the moment the balance tips
summary: A key-frame strip plus a hot-spot temperature history shows a warm patch slowly warming, then jumping to flame temperature at a sharp tipping point. Read the history for when the tipping happens and the strip for what it does in space.

media.alt: Top row: four temperature maps of a 20 by 20 millimetre domain at 0.0, 4.8, 6.6 and 24.0 milliseconds, titled before ignition, heat building up, ignition point and fully burning. A faint warm patch near the centre becomes a small bright spot at 6.6 ms and a round yellow burning kernel of about 11 mm diameter at 24 ms. Bottom left: the hottest-point temperature rises slowly from about 1250 K, jumps to about 2800 K at about 6.6 ms and stays there, while the average temperature rises from about 680 K to about 1080 K. Bottom right: percent of fuel consumed rising from 0 to about 25 percent.

source.caption: Hot-spot ignition: a warm patch turning into a self-sustaining flame
group: 08_rf_ignition_transient: Hot-spot ignition: a warm patch turning into a self-sustaining flame (representative, the only figure in this group)
source.note: Single-figure group. The figure names the in-house solver in its own title; no objective values or unpublished model details are shown, and the page teaches only the generic reading of ignition transients.

read_the_figure.question: At what time does a pre-heated patch stop being a hot patch and become a self-sustaining flame, and does the burnt region then keep growing?
read_the_figure.axes: Top row: x and y are position in millimetres on a 20 by 20 mm domain; colour is temperature in K, from about 300 to 3000. Bottom left: x is time in milliseconds, y is temperature in K, for the hottest point and for the domain average. Bottom right: x is time in milliseconds, y is the percentage of fuel consumed. The dashed vertical line in the lower panels marks the ignition time.
look_at: The hottest-point curve: a slow rise, then a near-vertical jump, then a plateau. The jump is the runaway.
The dashed line and the label ignition (runaway begins): it sits at the knee of the jump, about 6.6 ms, and matches the third key frame.
The average-temperature curve: it barely moves until the runaway and then climbs gently. A runaway in a small region barely changes the mean at first.
The fuel-consumed curve: nearly flat before the dashed line and rising steadily afterwards, so the burning region keeps consuming fuel on its own.
The last key frame: a sharp-edged round kernel, the edge being the flame front.
read_the_figure.proves: The pair of curves separates three states: a patch that is warming but not yet reacting fast, the tipping point, and a self-sustaining flame that continues to consume fuel after the initial heat is no longer needed. That is a computed ignition event with a flame front, not just a temperature rise.
if_wrong: A hot-spot curve that rises and falls back without a jump: the patch was below the ignition threshold and cooled by conduction.
A jump with fuel consumed staying flat: the temperature is prescribed or the chemistry is off.
An ignition time that changes strongly with grid or time step: the stiff chemistry is not resolved.
A kernel that fills the domain uniformly rather than having a front: the model is behaving as a homogeneous reactor, not a flame.
must_check: The ignition criterion is defined (here a vertical line is drawn but the rule that places it, such as a maximum temperature rise rate, is not stated).
The initial patch size and temperature, the mixture and the pressure are stated; only the 1250 K peak can be read from the curve.
Colour scale is the same in every key frame.
Time resolution near the jump is shown: the hot-spot curve has only a few points on its steep part.
Grid and time-step independence of the ignition time.
as_drawn: Read off the plot (about 5 percent): hottest-point temperature at t = 0 is about 1250 K; it is about 1500 K at 4.8 ms, about 1900 K at 6.0 ms, about 2800 K at 6.6 ms, and plateaus near 2900 K, ending near 2750 K at 24 ms.
The average temperature rises from about 680 K to about 1080 K over 24 ms.
Fuel consumed is about 1 percent at the dashed line (6.6 ms) and about 25 percent at 24 ms.
Kernel diameter at 24 ms is about 11 mm, from about 4.5 to 15.7 mm on the x axis.

terms.meaning: The transition from slow reaction to a self-accelerating one, in which heat release raises the temperature, which speeds the reaction further.
The positive feedback of rising temperature and rising reaction rate when heat generation outgrows heat loss.
A small region heated above its surroundings, for example by a spark or a hot particle.
The reaction rate increases exponentially with temperature through an activation energy.
The energy barrier of a reaction; a large barrier makes the rate extremely sensitive to temperature.
The thin moving layer separating burnt hot gas from unburnt cold gas.
Chemistry whose fastest time scales are far shorter than the flow, requiring implicit or specialised integrators.

remember: Ignition is a competition: heat released by reaction against heat lost by conduction.
Because the Arrhenius rate is exponential, a small temperature rise near the threshold can change the rate by a large factor.
Before runaway the average temperature barely changes; the hottest point is the diagnostic.
A flame is self-sustaining only if it keeps consuming fuel after the igniting heat is gone.
An ignition time without its criterion is not reproducible.

understand.title: Why there is a sharp knee
understand.text: Below a critical temperature the heat conducted away matches the heat released, so the patch drifts. Slightly above it, release exceeds loss; the temperature rises, the rate rises exponentially, and the temperature climbs by roughly a thousand kelvin in a fraction of a millisecond. The jump saturates at the burnt temperature when the local fuel is spent, which explains the plateau.

understand.title: Strip and curves together
understand.text: The strip shows where and the curves show when. The third frame at 6.6 ms catches the first bright spot, which is the same instant as the dashed line. Between frames two and three the patch stays warm, so the jump is localised rather than a heating of the whole domain.

understand.title: Why the average hardly moves
understand.text: The burnt kernel is small compared with the domain at the moment of runaway, so the area-averaged temperature has not yet felt it. It starts to rise afterwards, as the kernel grows.

steps.title: Arrhenius rate
steps.note: The exponential temperature dependence is the origin of the runaway.

steps.title: Heat balance of a patch
steps.note: Generation rises exponentially with T; loss rises roughly linearly. Ignition is when the two curves no longer cross.

steps.title: Linearise the exponent near the starting temperature
steps.note: This is the Frank-Kamenetskii approximation. It turns the Arrhenius rate into an exponential e^theta in the temperature rise, which is the shape of the early part of the jump.

steps.title: Runaway of the linearised problem
steps.note: Without loss, theta reaches infinity at a finite time t = 1/Lambda: a thermal explosion. In practice depletion of fuel stops it, which gives the plateau in the figure.

steps.title: Semenov criticality scale
steps.note: The temperature rise above the wall or ambient temperature at which loss can no longer balance generation. It is small when E_a / R is large: a high-activation-energy reaction needs only a small additional rise to tip.

steps.title: Ignition delay as the time to the knee
steps.note: An order-of-magnitude estimate: the time for generation at the initial temperature to heat the patch by the Semenov scale. It falls exponentially as T0 rises, which is why the Arrhenius plot of ignition delay against 1000/T is a straight line.

worked.title: Semenov temperature rise for an illustrative reaction
worked.problem: Illustration with assumed numbers, not read from the figure: a reaction with E_a/R = 15000 K in a patch at T0 = 1000 K. Estimate the temperature rise at which runaway starts.
worked.answer: About 67 K. With a higher activation energy the tipping rise is smaller. The figure itself does not give E_a, so this is a scale check, not a reading of the plot.

analyze.q: The average temperature curve shows no sign of the runaway at 6.6 ms. Why would a plot of only the average temperature miss ignition?
analyze.hint: Compare the sizes of the hot spot and the domain.

analyze.q: The hot-spot curve has only about three points on its steep part. What error does that introduce in the reported ignition time?
analyze.hint: The time of the knee could lie anywhere between two samples.

analyze.q: If the initial patch had been 100 K cooler, what would you expect for the hot-spot curve, and what does that tell you about a threshold?

evaluate.q: How would you define the ignition time in a way another person could reproduce?
evaluate.hint: A threshold on dT/dt or on the maximum temperature rise.

evaluate.q: Does 25 percent fuel consumed at 24 ms show a flame propagating? What else would you look at?
evaluate.hint: Front position against time, front speed.

create: Redraw the figure with the ignition criterion stated in the legend, markers on the time samples, and a log axis on the temperature rise.
Design a sweep over initial patch temperature that locates the ignition threshold and plot ignition time against it.

checks.q: Why does the hottest point jump while the average hardly changes?
checks.answer: The runaway is local; the burning kernel occupies a small fraction of the domain when it starts, so the area-averaged temperature barely responds.

checks.q: A reaction has E_a/R = 20000 K and starts at 1000 K. Estimate the Semenov rise.
The fuel-consumed curve is nearly flat before the dashed line. Why is that consistent with the temperature rising for 6 ms?
checks.answer: At low temperature the rate is very small, so little fuel burns even though the patch is warming; the rate becomes large only near the tipping point.

checks.q: A run shows a temperature jump to 2900 K but fuel consumed stays below 1 percent. Is it ignition?
checks.answer: Not demonstrated: the temperature is high but there is no evidence of ongoing reaction. Check that the heat release is coupled to the fuel consumption.

checks.q: How would you test for grid independence of the ignition time?
checks.answer: Repeat the run on at least two finer grids and smaller time steps with the same criterion, and show the ignition time converges.
